result: The manuscript establishes the fundamental role of titin in vertebrate sarcomere structure. Titin spans from the Z-disc to the M-band, mechanically linking actin and myosin filaments, ensuring sarcomeric integrity, and determining sarcomere length (~3 µm in relaxed human skeletal muscle).
evaluation: Claims C1-C5, C12-C17, C22-C23 collectively describe well-established knowledge about vertebrate titin structure and function, supported by multiple citations to established literature. These claims provide essential background context for the study.

result: Recent genetic and mechanical studies demonstrate that titin determines sarcomere dimensions and is responsible for passive muscle tension. Deletion of titin's I-band or A-band regions in mouse skeletal muscle resulted in corresponding shortening of sarcomeric I-band or A-band, and mechanical tension in relaxed muscle stretches titin into its extended conformation.
evaluation: Claims C18-C21 are supported by citations to recent published genetic and mechanical studies (Brynnel et al., 2018; Tonino et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; Linke, 2018; Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020; Swist et al., 2020). These provide important context for the titin ruler hypothesis.

result: In Drosophila and C. elegans, titin's role appears to be split between two proteins with distinct I-band and A-band features. Drosophila sarcomere lengths are stereotypic: ~3.5 µm in indirect flight muscles and ~8 µm in larval body wall muscles.
evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by citations to published literature and established knowledge about invertebrate muscle structure. This establishes the biological context and motivation for the current study.

result: Drosophila flight muscles achieve high stiffness through alternative splicing of titin homologs. The majority of stiffness is due to Sallimus, and flexible PEVK spring domains in both sls and bent genes are largely spliced out in adult flight muscles, as verified by transcriptomics analysis.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by citations to published literature (C27, C28) and by transcriptomics data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 (C29). The data directly support the splicing patterns claimed.

result: Confocal microscopy with fluorescently-labeled nanobodies reveals that N-terminal and C-terminal Sallimus nanobodies localize to single bands at Z-discs, while N-terminal Projectin nanobodies localize to Z-discs but C-terminal Projectin nanobodies localize to two bands at large distances from Z-discs.
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are directly supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 1B and 1D. The images clearly show the described banding patterns for each nanobody, providing initial localization data.

result: Projectin is present in an extended conformation in flight muscles, with a large part located along the myosin filament. This inference is based on the observed band positions and the established fact that the flight muscle I-band extends less than 100 nm from the Z-disc.
evaluation: Claims C34-C36 represent reasonable inferences from the confocal data (C33) combined with well-established measurements of I-band length from multiple cited studies (Burkart et al., 2007; Kronert et al., 2018; Loison et al., 2018; Reedy and Beall, 1993; Szikora et al., 2020).

result: DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy enables imaging at high spatial resolution with localization precision of 4-8 nm using the NeNA metric. The final epitope position measurements achieved 95% confidence intervals of only 1-8 nm through bootstrapping analysis.
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are supported by citations to DNA-PAINT literature (C93), the data analysis methods with citation to the NeNA metric (C94), and bootstrapping analysis shown in Figure 6B (C95). The precision estimates are appropriate for the method.

result: DNA-PAINT super-resolution reveals that Sallimus bridges across the entire flight muscle I-band. Sls-Ig13/14 is localized ~50 nm from the Z-disc center, and Sls-Ig51/Fn2 is ~50 nm farther toward the sarcomere middle, suggesting Sls mechanically links the Z-disc to the myosin filament similar to vertebrate titin.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 are supported by DNA-PAINT data in Figure 5A showing precise epitope positions. The inference that Sls bridges the I-band (C39, C6) is well-supported given the measured positions and known I-band length (<100 nm). C40 is appropriately presented as speculative.

result: DNA-PAINT reveals that Projectin is located at the beginning of the A-band in flight muscles. The N-terminus of Projectin is ~100 nm from the Z-disc at the beginning of the thick filament. Two-color DNA-PAINT shows Proj-Ig5-8 and Proj-Fn1/2 are separated by ~25 nm, with Proj-Ig27-Fn35 located 350 nm from the Z-disc.
evaluation: Claims C41-C45, C7 are directly supported by DNA-PAINT data shown in Figures 4A and 5B. The measurements are precise and consistent. The inference that Projectin is at the beginning of the A-band (C42, C7) is well-supported by the measured positions and cited I-band length.

result: The N-terminal part of Projectin is arranged in an extended, likely linear conformation reaching from the myosin filament into the I-band, running in parallel to the C-terminal domains of Sallimus.
evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are reasonable inferences based on the measured positions of multiple Projectin domains (C43-C45) showing a progressive increase in distance from the Z-disc, consistent with a linear extended structure.

result: Two-color DNA-PAINT reveals a staggered organization of Sallimus and Projectin with significant overlap at the I-band/A-band interface. Proj-Nano29 is ~15 nm farther from the Z-disc than Sls-Nano39, while in 42/45 sarcomeres, Proj-Nano30 is 7-8 nm closer to the Z-disc than Sls-Nano42.
evaluation: Claims C48-C50, C8-C9 are directly supported by two-color DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 5C and the composite sarcomere in Figure 6A. The measurements are precise and reproducible, clearly demonstrating the staggered overlap of the two proteins.

result: Despite variable sarcomere length (~3.5 µm), the distance between measured epitopes remains constant. Pooled data from all experiments places Proj-Ig5-8 at 90 nm and Sls-Ig49/50 and Sls-Ig51-Fn2 at ~98 nm from the Z-disc.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 (C51) and pooled analysis from all DNA-PAINT experiments (C52-C53). The constant epitope distances despite variable sarcomere length validate the pooling strategy.

result: The staggered architecture of Sallimus and Projectin may help stably anchor Sallimus at the myosin filament, ensure efficient force transduction during flight, and prevent sarcomere rupturing. Projectin may serve as an effective glue to connect Sls to the myosin filament.
evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C54, C87, C89, C92 are speculative interpretations of the observed staggered architecture. While the structural data (C48-C50) are solid, the functional implications remain hypothetical without direct mechanical or genetic testing. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('may', 'suggests').

result: The nanobodies efficiently penetrate large flight muscle fibers containing highly packed sarcomeres, which are among the most protein-dense macromolecular structures in biology.
evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are supported by the successful staining results throughout the manuscript and citations to published literature about sarcomere protein density (Daneshparvar et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2019).

result: Previous STORM studies located Sls-Ig16 ~50 nm from the Z-disc center, consistent with the current findings. Z-disc components α-Actinin and Zasp52 extend ~35 nm from the Z-disc center, while Filamin extends to ~55 nm, suggesting the N-terminus of Sls can reach and interact with these Z-disc components.
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by citations to a previous STORM study (Szikora et al., 2020) and represent reasonable inferences about potential Sls interactions based on spatial proximity. The inference in C60 is appropriately supported by cited biochemical studies.

result: The C-terminal end of Sls is located ~100 nm from the Z-disc center in flight muscles, where myosin filaments begin. This suggests Sls spans across the short flight muscle I-band and could interact with the myosin filament through its C-terminal domains, mechanically linking the Z-disc with the myosin filament.
evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by DNA-PAINT data (C61) and citations to previous STORM and EM studies establishing myosin filament position (C62). The inference about Sls spanning the I-band (C63) is well-supported by the combined data.

result: The C. elegans titin homolog TTN-1 bridges across the I-band reaching the A-band, and its C-terminal Ig38-40 domains bind myosin with low nanomolar affinity. This supports the hypothesis that Drosophila Sls may interact with myosin or Projectin and function as an I-band ruler.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by citation to published literature (Forbes et al., 2010). C66 is appropriately presented as a speculative hypothesis based on the observed architecture and comparison to C. elegans, providing evolutionary context.

result: A chain of 40 Ig domains would theoretically span ~160 nm, but the observed Sls length is only ~100 nm, suggesting the native Sls structure in the flight muscle I-band might be more complex than a straight linear array of Ig domains.
evaluation: Claims C67-C68 represent a valid calculation based on cited structural data (Mayans et al., 2001) and the observed measurements. The inference about structural complexity (C68) is reasonable given the discrepancy, though alternative explanations are not fully explored.

result: Non-flight muscles with long I-bands express longer Sls versions including PEVK domains. Sls is >2 µm long in larval muscles, strongly suggesting Sls determines I-band length in different muscle types, though direct genetic testing remains to be done.
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by citations to published literature (C69) and the accompanying paper (C70). The inference about Sls determining I-band length (C71) is appropriately presented as strongly suggested but requiring further genetic validation.

result: Projectin starts ~90 nm from the Z-disc in flight muscles, making direct interaction with Z-disc components unlikely. The N-terminus extends into the I-band, the first Fn/Ig super-repeat is at the A-band beginning (110 nm), and Ig-Fn super-repeats extend ~250 nm toward the M-band. Projectin alone likely cannot rule A-band length as it spans only ~15% of the myosin filament.
evaluation: Claims C72-C78 are supported by DNA-PAINT data throughout the manuscript. The inferences about Projectin's inability to interact with Z-disc components (C73) and rule A-band length (C78) are reasonable based on the measured positions and limited span along the myosin filament.

result: Drosophila flight muscles are very stiff to power wing oscillations at 200 Hz through a stretch-activation mechanism. Flight muscles express TpnC4 requiring stretch for activation, myosin experiences stretch-induced deformation, sarcomere contractions have ~3.5% amplitude (60 nm per half sarcomere), producing up to 110 W/kg power output.
evaluation: Claims C79-C84 are supported by established knowledge (C79) and multiple citations to published literature on flight muscle mechanics and physiology (C80-C84). These provide important functional context for interpreting the structural findings.

result: Sls is a candidate for storing elastic energy during flight muscle oscillations. Sls length would oscillate during flight, likely resulting in high oscillating forces across Sls.
evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are speculative inferences based on Sls's position bridging the I-band and the mechanics of muscle contraction. While plausible, these functional claims lack direct experimental support and are appropriately presented as speculative.

result: Flight-induced muscle ruptures occur when muscle-tendon attachment is weakened, underscoring high forces during flight. Both Sls and Projectin are needed to assemble contractile sarcomeres in larval muscles, and knockdown of either results in embryonic lethality and defective sarcomerogenesis.
evaluation: Claims C88, C90-C91 are supported by citations to published literature (Lemke et al., 2019; Loreau et al., 2023; Schnorrer et al., 2010). These provide important functional context supporting the importance of both proteins.
